title: Sampling Rates and Digital Aliasing Artifacts
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Explain why plotting f(x) = sin(20*pi*x) on the window [0, 5] using an under-sampled grid of 20 equally spaced points produces a misleading flat line or false frequency.
finalAnswer: \text{Period } T = 0.1; \quad \Delta x = 0.25 > T; \quad \text{Violates the Nyquist sampling theorem, creating severe aliasing.}

steps.title: Calculate the True Period of the Function
steps.explanation: The function completes 10 full cycles for every 1 unit of x, meaning there are 50 complete oscillations across the interval [0, 5].
steps.why: The fundamental period is 2*pi divided by the frequency coefficient B.

steps.title: Analyze the Sampling Step Size
steps.explanation: Evaluating at 20 points means sampling occurs every 0.25 units. Since Delta x = 0.25 is 2.5 times larger than the full period T = 0.1, the sampler misses entire wave cycles between adjacent pixels.
steps.why: Accurate digital plotting requires step size Delta x to be significantly smaller than half the period.

steps.title: Identify the Resulting Artifact
steps.explanation: Every sampled point evaluates to 0 because 5*pi*k is an integer multiple of pi. Consequently, connecting these sample points renders a completely flat horizontal line y = 0, misrepresenting the high-frequency oscillation.
steps.why: Aliasing occurs when sample frequencies coincide with integer multiple nodes of the true periodic signal.
